periods.activity_title: My Address on the Blue Planet
periods.textbook_anchor: The Blue Planet — Students fill in their full address from name to planet and discuss how their home fits into Earth's shared space (p. 162)
periods.visual_aids: Globe (for teacher demonstration of landmasses and oceans)

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up the globe and invites students to look at it quietly. She asks: 'What do you see — lines between countries, or something else?' Students share observations briefly. The teacher draws out the idea that from far away, Earth shows only land and water, no borders — just as Textbook p. 162 opens with astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla's reflection.

Students open Textbook p. 162 and read the address-filling activity. Each student writes their own address from their name all the way down to 'Planet: Earth' in their notebook. The teacher circulates, ensuring everyone reaches 'Planet' as the final line and pauses to ask: 'Which part of your address is shared with everyone in this room? Which is shared with all humans?'

Pairs share their addresses with each other, comparing how the entries differ at street and city level but converge at 'Planet: Earth'. The class discusses: 'Why does nature not show the borders we draw on maps?' The teacher introduces Wing Commander Rakesh Sharma's reply 'Saare Jahaan Se Achcha' and the DIGIPIN idea to anchor the conversation in real examples from the textbook.

Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'Earth is a shared home because ___.' The teacher collects two or three to read aloud, building a closing thought that air, water, seeds, and people move across the whole planet without stopping at any line.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how increasing the scale of an address — from local to planetary — reveals what is shared across all of humanity.
periods.section_context: Astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla's borderless Earth reflection, DIGIPIN, Wing Commander Rakesh Sharma's 'Saare Jahaan Se Achcha', globe showing landmasses and oceans, personal address from name to planet.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you could see your address from space, which part would still be visible?' This draws out the distinction between human-made divisions and natural features. Let students speak before introducing the textbook quotes.

periods.textbook_anchor: The Blue Planet — Students use a globe to find whether all oceans are connected and to locate India (p. 162)

time_bands.activity: The teacher places the globe at the front and asks: 'Before you touch it, predict — are all the oceans separate, or do they join up somewhere?' Students state their prediction in one sentence in their notebooks. This surfaces prior assumptions and gives the observation a purpose.

In small groups, students take turns tracing the oceans with a finger on the globe, following Textbook p. 162's instruction to find whether all oceans are connected. Each group records its finding in a simple two-column table: 'Ocean name — Connected to which ocean?' The teacher circulates with guiding questions but does not give the answer.

Groups share their findings. The class converges on the observation that all oceans form one continuous body of water. Students then locate India on the globe and note the ocean names surrounding it. The teacher asks: 'What does one connected ocean tell us about how water, animals, and ideas might move across the world?'

Students write two sentences in their notebooks: one recording the ocean-connectivity finding and one recording where India sits on the globe relative to those oceans. The teacher closes by linking the connected ocean to the chapter's idea that nature does not observe borders.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use a globe to identify and record a geographic feature and draw an inference about natural connectivity.
periods.section_context: Globe, connected oceans, India's location on the globe.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Let groups work at the globe without immediate teacher input so the discovery feel is preserved. Ask: 'Could a fish swimming in the Pacific eventually reach the Indian Ocean — why or why not?'

periods.textbook_anchor: Story 1: The Travelling Birds! — Students use a string on a globe to trace the rosy starling's migration route from Russia and Mongolia to India (p. 165)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the opening lines of Textbook p. 164 about rosy starlings arriving in India every winter. She asks: 'Where do you think these birds sleep at night during their journey? What might stop them — or help them?' Students predict briefly. The discussion establishes that wind, warmth, and food are navigational aids.

Pairs collect a length of coloured string and a globe. Following the activity on Textbook p. 165, they place one end of the string on Russia or Mongolia and stretch it to India, pressing it along the globe's surface to show the curved path. They observe which countries and water bodies lie along the route and record three observations in their notebooks: the rough distance covered, one country the birds pass over, and one water body they cross.

Pairs share their three observations with the group next to them. The teacher facilitates a brief whole-class comparison: 'Did different groups find different countries along the route? Why might the path vary?' The class discusses how birds find their way — linking the textbook's mention of warm climate and locust food supply to students' earlier predictions about wind and warmth.

Each student writes one sentence: 'The rosy starling's journey shows that nature connects ___ and ___ because ___.' The teacher invites two or three readings to close the unit on the idea that bird migration is a living demonstration of a borderless natural world.

periods.implied_lo: Students can trace a migration route on a globe and use geographic observations to explain how natural forces connect distant regions.
periods.section_context: Rosy starlings, Russia, Mongolia, India, winter migration, locusts and grasshoppers as food source, string-on-globe route tracing.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'In your community, do people notice when certain birds arrive each year? What do they call them?' This draws out local names and seasonal knowledge without labelling it as a special category.

periods.activity_title: A Bird's Postcard from the Sky
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 1: The Travelling Birds! — Students imagine they are a bird travelling the world and write a short postcard about what they see and what helps them on their journey (p. 165)
materials: half-sheet of paper or postcard-sized card

time_bands.activity: The teacher rereads the rosy starling story briefly from Textbook p. 164–165, pausing to ask: 'If you were flying over the ocean at night, what would you look for — warmth, food, land?' Students call out ideas freely. This oral warm-up fills the creative tank before writing begins.

Students each write a short postcard or note from the perspective of a bird mid-journey, as invited by Textbook p. 165. The postcard should describe: one thing they see below (a river, a city, a forest), one thing that is helping them (wind, warm air, ocean currents), and one feeling or thought about the journey. On the back of the card students draw a tiny sketch of what the bird sees. The teacher circulates, encouraging sensory detail.

Students pair up and read their postcards to each other, then the pair chooses one postcard to share with the class. Four or five postcards are read aloud. The teacher notes on the board the different helpers students named (wind, ocean currents, warm weather, food sources) and asks: 'What does this list tell us about how Earth's systems support living things that cross borders?'

Students stick or store their postcards in their notebooks. The teacher offers a closing thought: the rosy starling's journey is a letter nature writes every winter — no passport, no border check, just the pull of a warm land far away.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express their understanding of natural migration through a first-person creative piece that identifies environmental forces supporting long-distance travel.
periods.section_context: Rosy starling migration, wind, ocean currents, warm weather, postcard writing from bird's perspective.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Some students may not have seen migratory birds — invite them to imagine from the story's clues. Ask: 'What would surprise you most if you could fly over an ocean?' to unlock creativity for less-confident writers.

periods.activity_title: Yoga Travels the World — Discussion and Reflection
periods.section_ref: Story 2: Yoga—India's Gift to the World!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 2: Yoga—India's Gift to the World! — Students discuss why yoga became popular in so many countries (p. 167)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Has anyone here tried a yoga pose, or seen someone do yoga?' Students share briefly. She then reads aloud the opening paragraph of the yoga story from Textbook p. 167, establishing its 3,000-year history in India and its connection to bodily health, mental peace, and harmony with nature.

The class discusses the question from Textbook p. 167: 'Why do you think yoga became popular in so many countries?' The teacher facilitates by asking: 'What does yoga offer that is hard to find in a shop — what need does it meet?' Students connect the ideas of health, calm, and simplicity (needing no equipment). The teacher notes key reasons on the board as students name them.

Students write individually: one yoga pose they have tried or seen, and what they think it helps with — as prompted by Textbook p. 167. After writing, two or three students share. The teacher connects their responses to the broader idea: India's cultural and philosophical tradition became part of a global human heritage because it answered a universal human need.

The teacher introduces the UN's declaration of 21 June as the International Day of Yoga and asks: 'What does it mean for the whole world to set aside one day for a practice that began in India thousands of years ago?' Students offer one-word or one-phrase responses. The teacher closes by naming yoga as an example of an idea that crossed every border because it served every person.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how a cultural practice from one region gains global reach by meeting a universal human need.
periods.section_context: Yoga's 3,000-year history in India, mental peace and bodily health, global spread through travellers and scholars, UN International Day of Yoga on 21 June.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do you think yoga changed at all as it travelled — or did it stay exactly the same?' This opens a discussion about cultural exchange without requiring textbook-specific answers. Draw out that practices often adapt as they move.

periods.activity_title: Chilli's Long Journey — Tracing a Spice on the Globe
periods.section_ref: Story 3: Chilli—A Spice that Changed our Lives!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 3: Chilli—A Spice that Changed our Lives! — Students use a coloured string to trace the journey of chillies from South America to India on the globe (p. 168)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Imagine Indian cooking without chillies — what would change?' Students respond freely. She then asks: 'Where did the chilli plant actually come from?' Students guess. The teacher reads the key fact from Textbook p. 168: chillies originated in South America and arrived in India 400–500 years ago with Portuguese travellers. She notes that before chillies, black pepper was the primary spice.

In pairs, students open Textbook p. 168 and use a coloured string on the globe to trace the chilli's journey from South America to India. They note in their notebooks: the continent of origin, the approximate ocean crossed, and the country that brought it (Portugal). They also read the additional activity on Textbook p. 168, choosing one food — potato, tomato, peanut, or cashew — and jotting down what they already know about where it came from.

Pairs share their globe-tracing findings. The teacher asks one or two pairs to point to the route on the globe in front of the class. The class compares the chilli route to the rosy starling route traced earlier: 'Both journeys crossed oceans — but one was made by a bird and one was made by a plant travelling with people. What does that difference tell us about connection?'

Each student writes one sentence in their notebook: 'The chilli's journey from ___ to ___ changed Indian food by ___.' The teacher closes by noting that this pattern — a living thing travelling with human trade — will appear again in the next stories they encounter in this chapter.

periods.implied_lo: Students can trace the journey of a plant across continents on a globe and explain how human trade routes introduced new elements into local cultures.
periods.section_context: Chilli origin in South America, Portuguese traders, arrival in India 400–500 years ago, black pepper as earlier spice, globe string-tracing, potato, tomato, peanut, cashew as related travellers.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Ask your family tonight which spice or food they use most — do they know where it came from originally?' This gently links the elders-and-community strand. Regionally varied answers about spices and recipes are all valid.

periods.activity_title: Sweet Stories — Sugar, Rice, and the Travels of Taste
periods.section_ref: Story 4: The Sweet Story of Sugar!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 4: The Sweet Story of Sugar! — Students discuss which Indian food they would share with the world and what new food items might travel in the future (p. 169)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the key ideas from the sugar story on Textbook p. 169: India originated jaggery-making and sugar refining, which then spread globally through trade; before sugar, honey was the main sweetener; rice, mangoes, and bananas from India also travelled outward, while paper came from China. She asks: 'What do all of these have in common — bird, chilli, sugar, paper?' Students connect them as things that moved across the world.

The class discusses the first question from Textbook p. 169: 'If you could choose one Indian food to share with the world, what would it be?' Each student writes their choice and one reason in their notebook first, then shares. The teacher records the foods students name on the board without editing, building a class list that reflects the diversity of the room.

The class discusses the second question from Textbook p. 169: 'What kind of new food items do you think will travel in the future?' Students speculate freely — local snacks, regional sweets, street foods. The teacher asks: 'What would a food need — good taste, long shelf life, easy to carry — to travel well?' This moves students from recall to reasoning about conditions for cultural exchange.

Students write one sentence completing the thought: 'Every meal we eat is a story of journeys because ___.' Two or three are shared. The teacher closes with the textbook's insight: our meals carry flavours and stories from around the globe, and each bite is a small act of global connection.

periods.implied_lo: Students can reason about the conditions that allow foods and practices to travel across cultures and predict future patterns of exchange.
periods.section_context: Jaggery and sugar-refining originating in India, global spread through trade, honey as earlier sweetener, rice and mangoes from India, paper from China, discussion of one Indian food to share with the world.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'In your home, do you use jaggery, sugar, or both? Did your grandparents use the same thing?' This draws out the elder-knowledge strand naturally. All regional variations in sweeteners and foods are equally valid answers.

periods.activity_title: The Marigold's Migration — Festival Flowers Across Cultures
periods.section_ref: Story 5: The Mexican Marigold Moves into India!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 5: The Mexican Marigold Moves into India! — Students write why both Indian and Mexican cultures use marigolds during festivals (p. 170)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Where have you seen marigolds — at home, in a temple, at a wedding, at Diwali?' Students respond with their own experiences. She then asks: 'Do you think this flower always grew in India — or did it come from somewhere else?' After a brief discussion she reads the key fact from Textbook p. 170: marigolds originated in Mexico and travelled across the world to India.

Students read the marigold story from Textbook p. 170 individually or in pairs. They then write their response to the first question on Textbook p. 170: 'Why do you think both Indian and Mexican cultures use marigolds during their festivals?' The teacher circulates, prompting students to think about colour, abundance, and the human need for beauty and celebration.

Students share their written responses. The teacher notes common threads: vibrant colour, availability, cultural association with warmth and celebration. She then poses the second question from Textbook p. 171: 'Why do you think people in different countries include flowers in their celebrations?' This widens the lens from the marigold to the universal human practice of using nature in celebration.

Students write one closing sentence: 'The marigold's story shows that when something beautiful travels, it ___.' Two or three sentences are read aloud. The teacher closes by drawing the connection: just as birds, spices, and practices cross borders, so do symbols of beauty and meaning — the marigold became Indian not by force but by resonance.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify shared human practices across cultures and explain why elements from one culture become embedded in another.
periods.section_context: Marigold origin in Mexico, use in Indian temples, weddings, Diwali and other festivals, Mexican festival use, vibrant orange and yellow colour, cultural resonance across two traditions.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there a flower, food, or custom that is used the same way in your community and somewhere very far away?' This draws out the near-to-far connection and may surface regional flower traditions like the use of jasmine or lotus.

periods.activity_title: Indian Cows in Brazil — Animals that Cross Continents
periods.section_ref: Story 6: The Cows that Went to Brazil!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 6: The Cows that Went to Brazil! — Students find out the names of at least five different breeds of cows with help from a teacher or elder (p. 172)
materials: board and chalk/marker for class list

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the opening of the cow story from Textbook p. 171: Portuguese traders took Indian cow breeds — Gir, Kankrej, and Ongole — to Brazil, where they now supply more than three-fourths of Brazil's milk and appear on stamps and coins. She asks: 'What made these cows so valuable that they appear on money in another country?' Students speculate about hardiness, productivity, and climate fitness.

Students open Textbook p. 172 and work on the breed-finding activity. The teacher and any available elder or senior student serve as the knowledge source. Together, the class builds a list on the board: students call out breed names they know (from personal experience, family, or prior knowledge) while the teacher adds the three named in the story — Gir, Kankrej, Ongole — until at least five breeds are recorded. Each student copies the list into their notebook and writes one sentence about what makes a breed suited to a particular place.

Students read the second activity on Textbook p. 172 and begin a personal list: things in their home or school that may have come from another part of the world, covering clothing, food, sports, musical instruments, and trees as the textbook suggests. They write at least three items, noting the likely origin of each. This is observational inquiry — they draw on what they see around them.

Pairs compare their lists. The teacher asks: 'Was anything on your list a surprise?' Two or three surprises are shared with the class. The teacher closes by connecting the cow story to the earlier bird and plant stories: animals, like seeds and ideas, move with people — and wherever they go, they change the place they arrive in.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe familiar objects and animals in their environment, classify them by origin, and draw inferences about how living things and goods move across the world through human agency.
periods.section_context: Gir, Kankrej, and Ongole cow breeds, Portuguese traders, Brazil's dairy industry, Indian breeds on Brazilian stamps and coins, everyday items from different parts of the world.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone seen a cow that looks different from the usual — a different hump, colour, or size? What was it called?' This draws out local agricultural knowledge. Accept any regional breed names students or their families know.

periods.activity_title: The Web of Life — Mapping What Travels To and From India
periods.textbook_anchor: Web of Life — Students list things that came to India from other countries and those that travelled from India to the world, then trace their journeys on a map using two coloured strings (p. 173)
materials: Globe or large printed world map
two colours of string or wool
periods.visual_aids: Globe or large printed world map

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the opening lines of the Web of Life section from Textbook p. 173: all the stories — birds, yoga, chilli, sugar, marigold, cows — point to one truth: we are all connected. She asks: 'If you had to pick the single most surprising journey from everything you have read in this chapter, which would it be?' Students share quickly, no more than one sentence each.

In small groups, students open Textbook p. 173 and work on the two-column activity: listing things that came to India from other countries and things that travelled from India to the world. They draw on all the stories covered. Each group then uses two different coloured strings on the globe or map to trace at least three inward journeys and three outward journeys, pressing the strings from origin to destination. One student in each group records the routes in a simple table in their notebook.

Groups share their tables with the class. The teacher builds a combined class list on the board with two columns: 'To India' and 'From India'. The class checks whether any journey appeared in more than one group's list and whether any group found a route not covered in the main stories. The teacher asks: 'Looking at this map of connections, what does it suggest about which directions exchange happens — one way, or both ways?'

Each student writes one sentence: 'The web of life means ___.' Two sentences are read aloud. The teacher closes on the textbook's own words: people, animals, plants, and ideas travel, mix, and grow together — and caring for each other and the planet makes us part of that web.

periods.implied_lo: Students can organise multiple examples of cross-cultural exchange into a structured comparison and represent exchange routes spatially on a map.
periods.section_context: Birds, yoga, chilli, sugar, marigold, Indian cow breeds as examples of exchange; two-column list of journeys to and from India; two-colour string tracing on globe or map.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there something in your own home or family's life that came from far away — something your grandparents did not have?' This bridges the textbook's interview activity into the classroom.

periods.activity_title: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam — The World as One Family
periods.textbook_anchor: One Earth, One Family! — Students write what 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' teaches us and express its meaning in their own words (p. 176)

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' on the board and reads it aloud. She asks: 'Has anyone heard this phrase before — at home, in a prayer, on a building?' Students share briefly. She then reads the explanation from Textbook p. 176: the world is one family, and that family includes all people, animals, trees, rivers, air, and sky.

Students write their responses to the first two tasks on Textbook p. 176: 'What does Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam teach us?' and 'Write the meaning of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam in your own words.' The teacher encourages students to write in their own voice and not to copy the textbook sentence. She circulates and asks: 'Who else besides people belongs to this family, according to the textbook?'

Students share their written responses in pairs, then three or four are read to the class. The teacher compares them on the board: some may focus on people, some on nature, some on the idea of care. She then opens the third question from Textbook p. 176: 'How can we live like one big family, even when we are different?' This shifts from explaining a concept to imagining its practice.

Students each offer one idea for living as one family — spoken or written. The teacher collects these on the board as a class commitment wall. She closes with the textbook's point that Earth is the only known planet with life, and that caring for Earth is caring for every member of the family described in Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain a philosophical concept of shared belonging in their own words and connect it to observable responsibilities toward living things.
periods.section_context: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, world as one family including people, animals, trees, rivers, air and sky, Earth as only known planet with life, MoEFCC logo as symbol of nature-human balance.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Have you heard a similar idea in any story, song, or prayer from your community — the idea that everything is connected or that we belong to each other?' This draws out resonance with local wisdom traditions without labelling them.

periods.activity_title: How Ideas Travel — A Short Story of Change
periods.textbook_anchor: One Earth, One Family! — Students pick one idea and write a short story about how it might have travelled from one place to another long ago and how it helped people change their lives (p. 176)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reminds students of the chapter's pattern — yoga, chilli, marigold, cow breeds, sugar — each a story of something travelling and changing lives. She reads the 'Let us reflect' prompt from Textbook p. 176: pick one idea and write a short story about how it might have travelled from one place to another long ago and how it helped people change their lives or the way they think. She models one sentence of a possible story aloud to show what 'travelling idea' can mean.

Students choose their idea — it may be from the chapter (yoga, chilli, a bird's migration, the concept of sugar-making) or any other idea they find compelling. They write their short story in their notebooks. The teacher circulates, asking: 'Who is in your story — a trader, a traveller, a farmer, a bird?' and 'How did the people whose lives changed feel about it?' She encourages a beginning (where it started), a journey (how it moved), and an ending (what changed).

Students pair up and read their stories to each other. Each listener names one detail they found surprising or vivid. Four or five stories are shared with the class. The teacher notes on the board the range of ideas students chose and the variety of ways they imagined the journey — by sea, by bird, by trader — showing that the chapter's pattern is a template students can apply to many situations.

Students write the title of their story in large letters at the top of the page. The teacher closes by saying: every idea in this chapter had a name — rosy starling, chilli, yoga — and now each student's story adds one more name to the world's long list of travelling ideas.

periods.implied_lo: Students can construct a narrative that traces the movement of an idea or living thing across a historical journey and articulates the change it produced.
periods.section_context: Reflective story-writing about a travelling idea, yoga, chilli, sugar, marigold, cow breeds, or any idea the student chooses; journey structure (origin, path, change).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Some students may feel uncertain about 'making up' a story — tell them they can retell one of the chapter's own stories in their own voice with their own details. Ask: 'What would the people in the story think when they first saw or tasted this new thing?'

periods.activity_title: Caring for Our Earth — One Act, One Earth
periods.textbook_anchor: One Earth, One Family! — Students write one way they can care for the Earth (p. 176)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a quiet question: 'If Earth is your family's home — not just your country's, not just your city's, but the whole family's home from Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam — what happens to the home if no one cares for it?' Students respond briefly. She then reads the 'Let us reflect' prompt from Textbook p. 176: 'Write one way you can care for the Earth.'

Students write their response to the Textbook p. 176 prompt individually: one specific, concrete act of caring for the Earth that they personally can do. The teacher encourages specificity over generality — not 'save the environment' but 'carry my own water bottle so fewer plastic bottles are thrown away'. She circulates and prompts: 'Where would you do this — at home, at school, on the way to school?'

Students share their acts with the class. The teacher writes them on the board, grouping them loosely: acts that protect water, acts that protect air, acts that protect living things, acts that reduce waste. She asks: 'Looking at this list, which act — if done by every person on Earth — would make the biggest difference?' This moves from individual to collective thinking.

Students write the final Textbook p. 176 prompt: 'Identify an item that can travel from India to other parts of the world and write about it.' This closes the chapter on both its threads — caring for Earth and the continued flow of India's gifts to the world. Students share one or two sentences each. The teacher closes: the chapter began with an astronaut looking down at a borderless Earth — it ends with each student deciding how to care for that home.

periods.implied_lo: Students can translate the ethical principle of shared planetary belonging into a specific, personally committed act of environmental care.
periods.section_context: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam as ethical framework, writing one personal act of caring for the Earth, identifying an item travelling from India to the world, MoEFCC logo as symbol of nature-human balance.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there something people in your community already do to take care of the land, water, or animals — that your grandparents also did?' This grounds the reflection in existing practices rather than treating care as a new idea. All regional practices of environmental stewardship are valid.

assessment_items.question_text: Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla noticed that from space, Earth looked as if it had no borders. Which of the following best explains why national borders are invisible from space?

options.label: A
options.text: Astronauts cannot see clearly from space because the atmosphere blocks their view.

options.label: B
options.text: Borders are human constructs drawn on maps, not physical features on Earth's surface.

options.label: C
options.text: Borders are painted in very light colours and fade over time.

options.label: D
options.text: Earth is too small for borders to be visible at any distance.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item tests the distinction between human-made constructs and natural features — the core idea of The Blue Planet section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how increasing the scale of an address — from local to planetary — reveals what is shared across all of humanity.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses the concept of a border with a physical marking on land — a misconception that borders are physical features that simply cannot be seen from far away.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused the idea of atmospheric interference with the conceptual point about borders — a factual confusion about what the atmosphere does to visibility.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has misattributed the invisibility of borders to Earth's size rather than to their non-physical nature — a confusion between scale of observation and nature of the feature.

assessment_items.question_text: When students traced the oceans on the globe, they found that all the oceans on Earth are connected. What does this connectivity of oceans most directly show about Earth?

options.label: A
options.text: All oceans have the same depth and temperature.

options.label: B
options.text: Countries that share an ocean always share the same weather.

options.label: C
options.text: The oceans were created at the same time by the same natural event.

options.label: D
options.text: Water, and the living things in it, can move freely across the planet without being stopped by land borders.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item requires the student to move from the observation (oceans are connected) to the inference (movement across the planet is possible) — the cognitive step practised during the globe activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use a globe to identify and record a geographic feature and draw an inference about natural connectivity.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has recalled a surface-level fact about oceans (properties like depth or temperature) rather than drawing the inference about connectivity — a failure to move from observation to inference.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused geographic connectivity with a question of geological origin — misreading what the globe activity was designed to establish.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has made an incorrect causal link between shared ocean and shared weather — a plausible-sounding but unrelated conclusion not supported by the section content.

assessment_items.question_text: Rosy starlings fly thousands of kilometres from Russia and Mongolia to India every winter. Using what you found when you traced their route on the globe, explain two reasons why this journey is possible for the birds.
expected_elements: Reference to at least one natural force that helps the birds (warm climate in India, wind, or food supply such as locusts and grasshoppers).
Reference to the geographic continuity that makes the route possible — the birds cross land and water without any barrier stopping them.
A statement connecting the journey to the chapter's idea that nature has no borders.
assessment_items.annotation: Award credit for any two well-explained reasons drawn from the story and globe activity. Students who mention only 'warm weather' without a second reason should receive partial credit. Regional bird names and local observations about winter birds are acceptable additions.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace a migration route on a globe and use geographic observations to explain how natural forces connect distant regions.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

expected_elements: Reference to at least one natural force that helps the birds (warm climate in India, wind, or food supply such as locusts and grasshoppers).
Reference to the geographic continuity that makes the route possible — the birds cross land and water without any barrier stopping them.
A statement connecting the journey to the chapter's idea that nature has no borders.

assessment_items.task: You wrote a postcard as a bird flying from Russia or Mongolia all the way to India. Read your postcard again, or write a new one. Your postcard should describe: (1) one thing you see below as you fly, (2) one thing that is helping you on your journey — such as the wind, warm air, or food — and (3) one thought or feeling about making such a long journey. Add a small sketch on the back showing what the bird sees.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about: What does the land or ocean look like from high above? What pushes or guides you? What would it feel like to fly across a whole ocean? Use the rosy starling's story from the textbook to help you.
format_of_output: A small sketch on the reverse side of the card or below the writing
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether the student has used at least one accurate natural helper (wind, warm climate, food) from the chapter. The sketch is assessed for effort and connection to the writing — it need not be artistically detailed. All imaginative details beyond the textbook's content are welcome.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express their understanding of natural migration through a first-person creative piece that identifies environmental forces supporting long-distance travel.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student's ability to inhabit the perspective of a migratory animal and use chapter knowledge about natural forces — wind, warmth, food — to explain how migration is possible.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs students to three specific elements: visual observation from height, a named natural helper, and a personal reflection. A complete postcard addresses all three. A weak response names only one or gives vague answers like 'it was a long journey' without content detail.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names a specific natural helper (e.g., warm southerly winds, locusts as food in India), gives a vivid visual detail (a river delta, a forest), and expresses a genuine thought about the journey. Weak: generic ('I flew a long way'), no natural helper named, no visual detail.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find writing difficult may produce a longer sketch with labels. Students who know local names for migratory birds may use those — this enriches rather than departs from the task.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The postcard format mirrors the textbook activity and allows personal voice. The sketch consolidates spatial understanding from the globe-tracing work.

assessment_items.question_text: Yoga began in India about 3,000 years ago and is now practised in almost every country. Which of the following best explains why yoga spread across the world?

options.label: A
options.text: The Indian government made all countries practise yoga after 2015.

options.label: B
options.text: Travellers and scholars from India shared yoga because it met a universal human need for health and mental peace.

options.label: C
options.text: Yoga requires expensive equipment that India sold to other countries.

options.label: D
options.text: Yoga spread because it is similar to sports already popular in other countries.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. The item tests whether students can identify the mechanism of cultural spread — not force or commerce but a practice meeting a universal need — as established in the yoga story.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 2: Yoga—India's Gift to the World!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how a cultural practice from one region gains global reach by meeting a universal human need.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused cultural spread with trade in goods — a misconception that yoga's reach depended on selling equipment rather than sharing a practice.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused voluntary cultural adoption with governmental mandate — a misunderstanding of how cultural exchange works, possibly confusing the UN International Day declaration with compulsion.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused yoga's distinctiveness with similarity to existing practices — missing the chapter's point that yoga offered something different and universally needed.

assessment_items.question_text: The chilli plant came to India from South America about 400–500 years ago, brought by Portuguese travellers. Before chillies arrived, what did people in India use to add spice to food? And how did the chilli's arrival change Indian cooking?
expected_elements: Correct identification of black pepper as the spice used before chillies arrived.
A statement that the chilli became central to Indian cuisine after its arrival.
A connection to the chapter's idea that plants travel through human trade and become embedded in new cultures.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit for all three elements. Partial credit if the student names black pepper and describes the change but does not connect it to the broader pattern of cultural exchange. Students may add regional examples of chilli use — all are valid.

expected_elements: Correct identification of black pepper as the spice used before chillies arrived.

assessment_items.question_text: India gave sugar-making to the world, and India also received things from other parts of the world — paper from China, for example. Think about one food or item that India might share with the world in the future. Explain what it is, why you chose it, and what conditions would help it travel successfully to other countries.
look_for: The student names a specific food or item from India (not a generic answer like 'Indian things').
The student provides a reason for choosing it — linked to taste, usefulness, accessibility, or cultural value.
The student identifies at least one condition that would help the item travel — such as ease of preservation, wide appeal, trade routes, or technology.
The response connects to the chapter's pattern that things travel when they meet a need or resonate with people far away.
assessment_items.annotation: Strong responses will name a specific item, give a well-reasoned justification, and identify a realistic condition for travel. Accept any regionally specific Indian food or item — students from different parts of India will name different things, all valid. Do not penalise students for naming items that have already begun to travel globally (e.g., dal, roti, masala chai) if they reason about the future expansion.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can reason about the conditions that allow foods and practices to travel across cultures and predict future patterns of exchange.

competency.competency_text: Connects changes in the environment and the lives of their family and community, as communicated by elders and through local stories (changes in occupation, food habits, resources, celebrations, communication)

look_for: The student names a specific food or item from India (not a generic answer like 'Indian things').
The student provides a reason for choosing it — linked to taste, usefulness, accessibility, or cultural value.
The student identifies at least one condition that would help the item travel — such as ease of preservation, wide appeal, trade routes, or technology.
The response connects to the chapter's pattern that things travel when they meet a need or resonate with people far away.

assessment_items.question_text: The marigold originally came from Mexico, yet today it is used in Indian temples, weddings, and festivals. Which of the following best explains why the marigold became so deeply embedded in Indian culture?

options.label: A
options.text: Mexican marigolds are easier to grow than all other flowers in India's climate.

options.label: B
options.text: The Indian government ordered people to grow Mexican marigolds instead of other flowers.

options.label: C
options.text: The marigold replaced the lotus as India's national flower after it arrived from Mexico.

options.label: D
options.text: The marigold's vibrant orange and yellow colours resonated with Indian values of warmth, celebration, and spirituality.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item tests cultural resonance as a mechanism of adoption — a key concept in the marigold story. Option D is a chapter-relevant but factually incorrect distractor about national symbols.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 5: The Mexican Marigold Moves into India!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify shared human practices across cultures and explain why elements from one culture become embedded in another.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has defaulted to a government-mandate explanation — misunderstanding cultural adoption as top-down imposition rather than organic resonance.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has attributed the marigold's success to horticultural ease rather than cultural fit — a plausible agricultural misconception not supported by the section.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused the marigold's cultural prominence with official national-symbol status — a confusion between widespread cultural use and governmental designation.

assessment_items.question_text: Portuguese traders took Indian cow breeds — Gir, Kankrej, and Ongole — to Brazil. Today, these breeds supply more than three-fourths of Brazil's milk and appear on Brazilian stamps and coins. What does this story tell us about how animals move from one part of the world to another, and why that movement matters?
expected_elements: Recognition that animals move through human agency — specifically trade and travel — not on their own.
A statement about the value of the Indian breeds in Brazil — their productivity, hardiness, or suitability to Brazilian conditions.
A connection to the chapter's broader idea that living things enrich the places they move to.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit for all three elements. Partial credit if the student addresses movement by human agency and the value of the breeds but does not connect to the broader theme. Students who name additional cow breeds from their region are demonstrating enriched engagement — credit this.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 6: The Cows that Went to Brazil!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe familiar objects and animals in their environment, classify them by origin, and draw inferences about how living things and goods move across the world through human agency.

expected_elements: Recognition that animals move through human agency — specifically trade and travel — not on their own.
A statement about the value of the Indian breeds in Brazil — their productivity, hardiness, or suitability to Brazilian conditions.
A connection to the chapter's broader idea that living things enrich the places they move to.

assessment_items.question_text: From the stories in this chapter, give two examples of things that travelled FROM India to other parts of the world, and two examples of things that came TO India from other countries. For each example, name what travelled and where it went or came from.
expected_elements: Two correct examples of things that left India — such as: Indian cow breeds (to Brazil), yoga (to the world), sugar-making technique (global), rice and mangoes (other lands).
Two correct examples of things that arrived in India — such as: rosy starlings (from Russia/Mongolia), chilli (from South America via Portugal), marigold (from Mexico), paper (from China).
Each example should name the item and the direction of travel (origin and destination).
assessment_items.annotation: Award credit for any correct examples drawn from the chapter. Students need not give examples only from the named stories — if they identify a correct additional example from the chapter's content, it is valid. Partial credit for two correct examples (one in each direction) with one missing or incorrect.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can organise multiple examples of cross-cultural exchange into a structured comparison and represent exchange routes spatially on a map.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Two correct examples of things that left India — such as: Indian cow breeds (to Brazil), yoga (to the world), sugar-making technique (global), rice and mangoes (other lands).
Two correct examples of things that arrived in India — such as: rosy starlings (from Russia/Mongolia), chilli (from South America via Portugal), marigold (from Mexico), paper (from China).
Each example should name the item and the direction of travel (origin and destination).

assessment_items.question_text: 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' means the world is one family. According to this idea, the family includes not only all people but also animals, trees, rivers, air, and sky. Do you think this idea can change the way people behave toward the environment? Use at least two examples from the chapter to support your answer.
look_for: A clear statement of what Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam means — the world as one family including all living and natural things.
A reasoned argument for how this idea can (or could) change behaviour toward the environment — not just a restatement of the concept.
At least two chapter-based examples used as evidence — e.g., caring for migratory birds, protecting forests so seeds can travel, not polluting oceans that connect the world.
Personal voice — the student's own reasoning, not a copied sentence from the textbook.
assessment_items.annotation: Strong responses connect the philosophical idea to specific behavioural change using chapter evidence. Accept any chapter-based examples — the student is not limited to the three suggested in the guide. Responses in regional languages or with regional examples of environmental care are equally valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain a philosophical concept of shared belonging in their own words and connect it to observable responsibilities toward living things.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

look_for: A clear statement of what Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam means — the world as one family including all living and natural things.
A reasoned argument for how this idea can (or could) change behaviour toward the environment — not just a restatement of the concept.
At least two chapter-based examples used as evidence — e.g., caring for migratory birds, protecting forests so seeds can travel, not polluting oceans that connect the world.
Personal voice — the student's own reasoning, not a copied sentence from the textbook.

assessment_items.task: Choose one idea, food, animal, or practice from this chapter — or any other that interests you. Write a short story (8–12 sentences) about how it might have travelled from one place to another a long time ago. Your story should have: a place where it started, a journey (who carried it, how it moved, what happened along the way), and an ending that shows how it changed the lives of the people it reached.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about: Who first noticed this thing or idea? Who carried it on a journey — a trader, a bird, a traveller? What did people think when they first saw or tasted it? How did it change their lives or the way they thought about the world?
assessment_items.annotation: Assess for: a clear origin, an identifiable journey, and a stated change produced. The student may choose any example from the chapter — yoga, chilli, sugar, marigold, rosy starling, cow breeds — or an example from their own knowledge. Stories that use regional detail or family knowledge are especially strong. Do not penalise for length if the three structural elements (origin, journey, change) are present.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a narrative that traces the movement of an idea or living thing across a historical journey and articulates the change it produced.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student's ability to apply the chapter's core pattern — origin, journey, change — to construct an original narrative, showing that they have internalised the idea of global exchange rather than memorised individual stories.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts three structural beats: who first held this thing, who carried it and how, and what changed when it arrived. A complete story addresses all three. A weak story summarises one chapter story without adding any narrative structure.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: original narrative voice, clear structure (origin-journey-change), specific sensory or emotional detail, chosen example used accurately. Weak: retells a chapter summary as bullet points, no journey described, no change articulated.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find sustained writing difficult may write fewer sentences if the three structural elements are present. Students may use a home language phrase or regional detail — this enriches the story. Students who choose an example not in the chapter are welcome to do so if they can explain its journey.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The story format mirrors the chapter's own mode of presenting exchange — each section is a story. Writing in this form develops the same organisational thinking the chapter models.

assessment_items.task: Think about Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam — the idea that the world is one family, including all people, animals, trees, rivers, air, and sky. Choose ONE specific action you will take to care for a member of this family — it could be a plant, an animal, water, air, or a person who needs help. Write: (1) what action you will take, (2) which member of the Earth-family you are caring for, and (3) why this action matters for the whole family, not just for you.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about: What is one small but real thing you can do? Who or what will be better because of it? How does taking care of one part of the Earth family help everyone else?
format_of_output: The name of the Earth-family member being cared for, written as a heading
assessment_items.annotation: The action must be specific and feasible within the student's own life — not 'save the planet' but a concrete act. All actions are valid regardless of scale. Responses that name regional or community practices of environmental care (a local tradition of not cutting certain trees, a water-conservation practice) are especially strong. Accept responses in any form the student can manage.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can translate the ethical principle of shared planetary belonging into a specific, personally committed act of environmental care.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student's ability to move from an abstract philosophical principle (Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam) to a concrete personal commitment — the application of an ethical idea to real behaviour.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold asks for three things: the action, the beneficiary (a named Earth-family member), and the reason it matters for the whole family. A complete response addresses all three. A weak response states a vague intention ('I will be good to nature') without naming an action or a beneficiary.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific action named ('I will not pour waste water into the drain near my school'), named beneficiary ('the river'), and a systemic reason ('because the river flows to the ocean which all living things depend on'). Weak: vague action, no beneficiary named, no connection to the wider family.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot write at length may draw the action with a one-sentence label. Students who describe a practice they already do at home or in their community are demonstrating existing engagement — credit this fully.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Short reflective written commitment with heading
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The reflective format matches the 'Let us reflect' prompt from the textbook and emphasises personal agency — the chapter's closing move from understanding to action.
